headline: From leaked secret to stolen data: five minutes.

slides.html:
From leaked secret to stolen data: five minutes.

Attackers are using AI agents to find and abuse exposed credentials. Your response time just changed.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence · 5 Nov 2026

An agent did the attacker’s legwork.

In one observed case, an AI agent went from scanning GitHub for client secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in about five minutes.

No human had to read the code, test the credential or work out what it could reach. The tooling did all three.
The five-minute chain

Deleting the file does not un-leak the secret.

Git keeps history. Forks and clones keep copies. Automated scanners may have read it within minutes.

Microsoft’s guidance is blunt: treat any credential that was ever public as compromised — even after the file is edited.

The fix is rotation, not a cleanup commit.

Change the defaults, not just the habits

INSTEAD OFMOVE TOClient secrets in configManaged identitiesHoping nobody commits keysSecret scanning + push protectionBroad app permissionsLeast-privilege roles per appLong-lived secretsShort maximum lifetimesEdit the file and move onRotate everything it could reach

Put it in the plan, not the wiki

This is not only a security team problem. It is a delivery problem: who owns the secret, how fast can you rotate it, and does your pipeline block the next leak?

→ Add push protection to the definition of done
→ Name an owner for every service identity
→ Rehearse a rotation before you need one

Remember this

The gap between leak and breach is now measured in minutes.

A public secret is a compromised secret. Rotate it.

The best secret is one that never exists — use managed identities.

How long would it take your team to rotate a leaked production secret?

Minutes, hours or days? Be honest in the comments.
